pr_title: daemon/logger: read the length header correctly
pr_body:
Before this change, if Decode() couldn't read a log record fully,
the subsequent invocation of Decode() would read the record's non-header part
as a header and cause a huge heap allocation.

This change prevents such a case by having the intermediate buffer in
the decoder struct.

Fixes #42125.

Signed-off-by: Kazuyoshi Kato <katokazu@amazon.com>

"closes #xxxx"

Please provide the following information:
-->

**- What I did**

Changing decoder struct to fix #42125.

**- How I did it**

Changing decoder struct to keep read-but-unused bytes.

**- How to verify it**

Run `docker logs -f $(docker run --rm -d --log-driver local alpine cat /dev/urandom) > /dev/null`. It kills dockerd after a few minutes before the change.

issue_context.title: OOM when following "local" logs of high-log-output container
issue_context.body:
**Description**

When logging to the `local` driver, Docker will quickly run out of memory when following the logs of a container with a lot of log output.

This also occurs when following local logs while using a driver such as `syslog` that supports dual logging.

This issue appears to be similar or identical to #39963.

**Steps to reproduce the issue:**
1. Run a container that logs heavily to the `local` driver:

    ```
    ID=$(docker run --rm -d --log-driver local alpine cat /dev/urandom)
    ```
2. Follow the container's logs:

    ```
    docker logs -f $ID > /dev/null
    ```

Alternatively:

1. Run a container that logs heavily to a driver that supports dual logging:

    ```
    ID=$(docker run --rm -d --log-driver syslog --log-opt syslog-address=udp://127.0.0.1:0 alpine cat /dev/urandom)
    ```
2. Follow the container's logs:

    ```
    docker logs -f $ID > /dev/null
    ```

**Describe the results you received:**
`dockerd` exits with `fatal error: runtime: out of memory`.

Stack trace: https://gist.github.com/2f674f1ff24c679ba4778f458facb7b2

**Describe the results you expected:**
Docker remains stable and keeps a reasonable memory footprint.

**Additional information you deem important (e.g. issue happens only occasionally):**
I have been unable to reproduce the issue when logging to the `json-file` driver.

At work we're running docker containers managed by Hashicorp Nomad, and use the `fluentd` log-driver in our docker daemon config. We've had the same issue with dockerd's memory usage ballooning over time, but we found we could prevent this using the following daemon.json setting:

```
  "log-opts": {
    "cache-disabled": "true",
```

[This disables Docker's "dual-logging" feature](https://docs.docker.com/config/containers/logging/dual-logging/#disable-the-dual-logging-cache), which creates a local log cache for log drivers that don't support local reads. Although this fixes the memory usage issue, it breaks the `docker logs` and `nomad alloc logs` commands. We decided we were fine with this compromise, because we already backup logs to a local file using fluentbit.

Before we made this change, over the course of a few hours dockerd would climb to 3 GB memory usage. After making the change it uses a steady ~240 MB. Hope others find this useful.

What is your Go version on `docker version`?

From Go 1.12 to Go 1.15, Go was using MADV_FREE to ask OS to reclaim memory. However it was not updating many userland-surfacing statistics (including RSS) and causing a lot of confusion. So in Go 1.16, the behavior has changed again to use MADV_DONTNEED instead.

https://github.com/golang/go/commit/05e6d28849293266028c0bc9e9b0f8d0da38a2e2

Note that moby/moby's Dockerfile is using Go 1.13.15 in 20.10.7.

Interesting, what affect would this have? Wrong pprofs and we'd need to regenerate them using a newer go version?

Sorry. No. Decode is not assuming that the current position of the file is the beginning of a record. EOF errors from Decode is ignored like below.

https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/a17f288e65b45a9f4aa54526817ba83220a59709/daemon/logger/loggerutils/logfile.go#L706-L735

However allocating a buffer based on `binary.BigEndian.Uint32(d.buf[:read])` is still problematic and potentially kills dockerd due to `fatal error: runtime: out of memory`.

The value we are reading in this section you mentioned is literally the size of the record.

The biggest each log entry can be is 1MB.
Add the protobuf encoding and whatever metadata (timestamp, explicitly specified container labels).
These are not unbounded.
We could look at chunking the records somehow so they do not exceed some pre-determined buffer size.

I am surprised that you would see a buffer of 71MB and would be curious what the data in that file looks like.

I was doing `docker run --rm -d --log-driver local alpine cat /dev/urandom` as @dnrce suggested. So this would be too harsh and less realistic.

That being said, IIUC `d.buf[:read]` in Decode() could point literally anywhere in a protobuf-encoded log stream file. Since protobuf embeds UTF-8 strings as is, if a log message contains `abcd` (in UTF-8, `0x61 0x62 0x63 0x64`), is there a possibility of allocating 0x61626364 bytes -> 1633837924 bytes -> 1.6GB?

@kzys No we write the log stream as `<record len><record><record len>`, which makes it easy to read both backwards and forwards.
So what's happening there when we set the buffer like above is we are reading `<record len>`.
Those lengths have a fixed size.

When io.ReadFull() below doesn't read the bytes fully (returning ErrUnexpectedEOF), the next invocation of Decode() must not decode the record header.

https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/a17f288e65b45a9f4aa54526817ba83220a59709/daemon/logger/local/read.go#L179-L190

The only thing I can imagine is that `readFull` returns `EOF` as shown in your log and now you have read half a msg length from the buffer? and now the next `Decode()` would be in the middle somewhere

EDIT:// EOF Should only be returned when no bytes are read at all, so this should not happen either.

Oh that could be it: What happens in `decodeLogEntry` might be the following. Assume there is a message length of 100.

 * The first `readFull` reads 50 bytes because there are only 50 bytes available and set `ErrUnexpectedEOF`
 * The second `readFull` reads 0 bytes and sets `EOF` because we are still at the end of the filestream.
 
Now we return with the error `EOF` and the next decode is in the middle of the stream and tries to read the message length again. Does that make any sense @kzys & @cpuguy83?

This is kind of a strange condition.

> If an EOF happens after reading some but not all the bytes, ReadFull returns ErrUnexpectedEOF

But we write the whole record in one shot.
So maybe the cursor is getting off somewhere else, or perhaps some weird fs behavior.

I think we should likely use ReadAt, track the cursor ourselves, and only advance after the cursor after a successful proto unmarshal.

> I think we should likely use ReadAt, track the cursor ourselves, and only advance after the cursor after a successful proto unmarshal.

Yes, something like this is certainly the safest approach. Returning from `Decode` before the whole message is read just cries for issue (at least as soon as the reader state/seek position is advanced)

I've opened #43043. 

> But we write the whole record in one shot. So maybe the cursor is getting off somewhere else, or perhaps some weird fs behavior.

I'm not entirely sure an atomic write could guarantee a corresponding atomic read.
